As noted in [LSS25, FKO⁺25], calibration with a distance measure $D$ that corresponds to a Bregman divergence can be written as a full swap regret with loss functions given by the associated proper scoring rule. Given a convex function $R : \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}$, the Bregman divergence associated to $R$, $D_R : \mathcal{P} \times \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, is defined as⁷

$$D_R(y \| p) := R(p) - R(y) - \langle \nabla R(y), p - y \rangle.$$

Geometrically, this divergence is defined by taking the hyperplane tangent to $R$ at $p$ and computing the difference in height between $R$ and the hyperplane at $y$ (see Figure 2).

When viewed as a loss function in $p$, the Bregman divergence $D_R(y \| p)$ also has the property that it is a proper scoring rule. This refers to the fact that if $y$ is drawn from some distribution $\mathbf{y} \in \Delta(\mathcal{P})$, the optimal response $p$ (to minimize the expected loss $D_R(y \| p)$) is simply the expectation $\bar{y} = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[y]$. In particular, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 2.1. For any $\mathbf{y} \in \Delta(\mathcal{P})$ and convex function $R : \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}$, let $\bar{y} = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[y]$, and $\overline{R(y)} = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[R(y)]$. For all $p \in \mathcal{P}$, $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[D_R(y \| p)] = D_R(\bar{y} \| p) + \overline{R(y)} - R(\bar{y})$. In particular, $\ell(p) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[D_R(y \| p)]$ is minimized at $p = \bar{y}$ at a value of $\overline{R(y)} - R(\bar{y})$ (Figure 3).

We say that a convex function R : 𝒫 → ℝ is α-strongly convex with respect to a given norm ‖·‖ if for any points y, p ∈ 𝒫 it is the case that
R(y) ≤ R(p) + ⟨∇R(p), y − p⟩ + α‖y − p‖².
Equivalently, the Bregman divergence must satisfy D_R(y ∥ p) ≥ α‖y − p‖². Thus, ‖·‖²-calibration error is bounded by D_R-calibration error if R is ‖·‖-norm 1-strongly convex.

Proof of Lemma 2.4. Note that if we define \mathcal{L} = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^d \mid \|y\|_* \le 1\} to be the unit dual-norm ball for some norm \|\cdot\|, then by duality the norm \|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{L}^*} corresponding to \mathcal{L}^* is simply the original norm \|\cdot\|. It therefore suffices to show that given a 1-strongly convex function R with bounded range \rho, it is possible to construct a 1-strongly convex function R' with bounded Bregman divergence O(\rho) (and vice versa).

Assume R is 1-strongly convex and satisfies \max_{p\in\mathcal{P}} R(p) - \min_{p\in\mathcal{P}} R(p) = \rho. Define R'(p) = 4\,R\!\left(\frac{p}{2}\right) (since \mathcal{P} is centrally symmetric, p/2 \in \mathcal{P}). If R is 1-strongly convex, then R(p/2) is 1/4-strongly convex, and so R' is also 1-strongly convex. We claim the maximum Bregman divergence of R' is at most O(\rho). To show this, first note that for any z_1, z_2 \in \mathcal{P}, \langle \nabla R(\tfrac{z_1}{2}), z_2 \rangle \le 2\rho. Indeed, since R is convex and has range bounded by \rho, we have \rho \ge R(x) - R(\tfrac{z_1}{2}) \ge \langle \nabla R(\tfrac{z_1}{2}), x - \tfrac{z_1}{2} \rangle for all x \in \mathcal{P}. Setting x = \tfrac{z_1 + z_2}{2} then gives \langle \nabla R(\tfrac{z_1}{2}), z_2 \rangle \le 2\rho. Now, note that
\max_{y,p\in\mathcal{P}} D_{R'}(y\,|\,p) = R'(y) - R'(p) - \langle \nabla R'(p), y - p \rangle
= 4\,R\!\left(\tfrac{y}{2}\right) - 4\,R\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right) - 2\left\langle \nabla R\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right), y - p \right\rangle
\le 4\left| R\!\left(\tfrac{y}{2}\right) - R\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right) \right| + 2\left( \langle \nabla R\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right), y \rangle - \langle \nabla R\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right), p \rangle \right)
\le 4\rho + 4\rho = 8\rho.

D.2 Lower bound for $\ell_2$ calibration

Next, we prove a lower bound for $\ell_2$ calibration.

Theorem D.2. There is a sufficiently small constant $c > 0$ so that the following holds. Write $D(p, p') = \|p - p'\|_2$ and fix any $\epsilon > 0, d \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for any $T \leq \exp(c \cdot \min\{d^{1/14}, \epsilon^{-1/7}\})$, there is an oblivious adversary producing a sequence $y_1, \ldots, y_T \in \mathcal{B}^d_2$ so that for any learning algorithm producing $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_T \in \Delta(\mathcal{B}^d_2)$, $\text{Cal}^D_T(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) \geq \epsilon \cdot T$.

Proof. Fix $\epsilon > 0, d \in \mathbb{N}$, and write $\tilde{\epsilon} = \epsilon^{6/7}$. We may assume without loss of generality that $d \leq \tilde{\epsilon}^{-14/6}$, so that $\min\{d^{1/14}, \tilde{\epsilon}^{-1/6}\} = \min\{d^{1/14}, \epsilon^{-1/7}\} = d^{1/14}$: if this were not the case, we simply use the adversary resulting from $\tilde{\epsilon}^{-14/6}$ dimensions and project the forecaster's predictions down into this lower-dimensional subspace, which can only decrease calibration error. Now suppose to the contrary that there was an algorithm Alg which bounded calibration error by $\epsilon T$ for $T \leq \exp(c \cdot \min\{d^{1/14}, \epsilon^{-1/7}\}) = \exp(c \cdot d^{1/14})$. Then by Lemma 4.2 with $\mathcal{P} = \mathcal{B}^d_2$ and norm $\|\cdot\| = \|\cdot\|_2$, for any subset $\mathcal{P}' \subset \mathcal{B}^d_2$ we get that there is an algorithm which chooses $\mathbf{x}'_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}'_T \in \Delta(\mathcal{P}')$ and which ensures that for every oblivious adversary choosing $y_1, \ldots, y_T \in \mathcal{B}^d_2$, we have
$$\text{FullSwapReg}_T(\mathbf{x}'_{1:T}, (\langle \cdot, y_1 \rangle, \ldots, \langle \cdot, y_T \rangle)) \leq \epsilon \cdot T. \tag{12}$$

On the other hand, the oblivious adversary of Theorem 4.1 guarantees a subset $\mathcal{X} \subset [-1,1]^d \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and an oblivious adversary producing a sequence $v_1, \ldots, v_T \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|v_t\|_\infty \leq d^{-13/14}$ for all $t \in [T]$, so that
$$\text{FullSwapReg}_T(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}, (\langle \cdot, v_1 \rangle, \ldots, \langle \cdot, v_T \rangle)) \geq \tilde{\epsilon} \cdot T \tag{13}$$
as long as $T \leq \exp(c_{4.1} \cdot d^{1/14})$. Theorem E.1 (Pure calibration error). Let P ⊂ ℝ^d be a bounded convex set and ‖·‖ be an arbitrary norm with unit dual ball L := { f ∈ ℝ^d | ‖f‖_* ≤ 1 }. Then, SampleTreeCal (Algorithm 3, with an appropriate choice of parameters H, L, S) guarantees that for an arbitrary sequence of outcomes y_1, …, y_T ∈ P, the ‖·‖^2 calibration error of its predictions x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(P) is bounded as follows:
E[PureCal_T^{‖·‖}(p_{1:T}, y_{1:T})] ≤ ε T, for T ≥ Rate(L, ‖·‖_*) · (diam_{‖·‖}(P)/ε)^{O(Rate(P, ‖·‖)/ε^2)}.

$$= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}}\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{T}(p - y_t) \cdot \mathbb{1}[p_t = p]\right\|\right]$$
$$\leq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}}\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{T/S}\sum_{j=1}^{S}(p - y_{S(i-1)+j}) \cdot \mathbf{x}_i(p)\right\| + \sum_{i=1}^{T/S}\sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}}\left\|\sum_{j=1}^{S}\big((p - y_{S(i-1)+j}) \cdot (\mathbb{1}[p_{S(i-1)+j} = p] - \mathbf{x}_i(p))\big)\right\|\right]$$
$$\leq 2\epsilon T.$$
The result follows by rescaling ε and our choice of L = O(\operatorname{Rate}(\mathcal{P}, \|\cdot\|)/\epsilon^2). □

Three presentational issues, none of which I can turn into a confident error: the prose announces a '$\|\cdot\|^2$ calibration error' while the display bounds $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{PureCal}_T^{\|\cdot\|}]$; the symbol $L$ denotes both the tree depth and the loss set $\mathcal{L}$ within the same statement; and the second worked example reports $(1/\epsilon)^{O(1/\epsilon^2)}$ as $\exp(O(1/\epsilon^2))$, suppressing a $\log(1/\epsilon)$. results.content:
We study the online calibration of multi-dimensional forecasts over an arbitrary convex set $\mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ relative to an arbitrary norm $\|\cdot\|$. We connect this with the problem of external regret minimization for online linear optimization, showing that if it is possible to guarantee $O(\sqrt{\rho T})$ worst-case regret after $T$ rounds when actions are drawn from $\mathcal{P}$ and losses are drawn from the dual $\|\cdot\|_*$ unit norm ball, then it is also possible to obtain $\epsilon$-calibrated forecasts after $T = \exp(O(\rho/\epsilon^2))$ rounds. When $\mathcal{P}$ is the $d$-dimensional simplex and $\|\cdot\|$ is the $\ell_1$-norm, the existence of $O(\sqrt{T \log d})$-regret algorithms for learning with experts implies that it is possible to obtain $\epsilon$-calibrated forecasts after $T = \exp(O(\log d/\epsilon)) = d^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ rounds, significantly improving upon the recent result of [Pen25].

Finally, we prove that any online calibration algorithm that guarantees $\epsilon T$ $\ell_1$-calibration error over the $d$-dimensional simplex requires $T \geq \exp(\Omega(1/\epsilon))$ (assuming $d \geq \text{poly}(1/\epsilon)$). This strengthens the corresponding $d^{\Omega(\log 1/\epsilon)}$ lower bound of [Pen25], and shows that an exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$ is necessary. Moreover, our lower bound is tight up to constant factors in the exponent, matching our upper bound.
results.route_rationale: A headline quantitative claim that can be checked by substituting the paper's own parameters into the paper's own formula.
results.reasoning: The abstract is inconsistent with itself and with the body on the paper's headline rate. (i) Its own general statement is $T = \exp(O(\rho/\epsilon^2))$; substituting the negative-entropy rate $\rho = \log d$ gives $\exp(O(\log d/\epsilon^2)) = d^{O(1/\epsilon^2)}$, yet the next clause reports $T = \exp(O(\log d/\epsilon)) = d^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ — one power of $\epsilon$ short. (ii) Section 1.1's own bullet reads '$(1/\epsilon)^{O(\log d/\epsilon^2)} = d^{O(1/\epsilon^2)}$. This recovers the result of [Pen25]', and Appendix E repeats '$T \ge d^{O(1/\epsilon^2)}$ ... recovers the main upper bound of [Pen25]'. The abstract's claim to be 'significantly improving upon the recent result of [Pen25]' therefore contradicts the body, which claims only to recover it. (iii) The abstract reports the lower bound as $T \ge \exp(\Omega(1/\epsilon))$, but Theorems 1.4 and 4.3 give $\exp(\Omega(\epsilon^{-1/6}))$ under the abstract's own hypothesis $d \ge \mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)$. (iv) The closing claim that the lower bound is 'tight up to constant factors in the exponent, matching our upper bound' cannot hold: the upper bound's exponent is $\Theta(\rho\epsilon^{-2}\log(\mathrm{diam}/\epsilon))$ and the lower bound's is $\Theta(\epsilon^{-1/6})$.

results.route_rationale: A hypothesis-matching question between an informal restatement and the formal theorem it restates; resolved by comparing the two definitions §2.4 sets up.
results.reasoning: Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 hypothesise that $R$ is 1-strongly convex with *range* $\max_x R(x) - \min_x R(x) \le \rho$, and Theorem 1.1 stresses 'no restrictions on symmetry'. But Theorem 3.1, which they restate, is stated in terms of $\mathrm{Rate}(\mathcal{P},\|\cdot\|)$, defined in §2.4 as the infimum over 1-strongly convex $R$ of the range of the *Bregman divergence* $\max_{y,p}D_R(y\|p)$. Section 2.4 says outright that 'these two quantities do not directly bound each other', giving negative entropy on the simplex as the counterexample — bounded range, unbounded Bregman divergence — and the bridge between them, Lemma 2.4, is proved only for centrally symmetric $\mathcal{P}$. So the informal statements drop a hypothesis the proof needs. The same gap affects the first worked bullet of §1.1, which invokes negative entropy with 'range $\rho = \log d$' on the simplex (not centrally symmetric) — precisely §2.4's counterexample. The conclusion is very likely still true for the simplex by a separate argument, which is why I rate this a gap in the stated hypotheses rather than a false claim.

findings.evidence: Lean compiled a proof of the **negation** of Lemma 2.1 as literally stated, read against the Bregman divergence defined in §2.3. Witness: $R(x)=x^4$ (convex, differentiable), $\mathbf{y}$ uniform on $\{0,1\}$ so $\bar y = 1/2$, and $p=0$. With $D_R(y\|p)=R(p)-R(y)-\langle\nabla R(y),p-y\rangle$ the left-hand side $\mathbb{E}_y[D_R(y\|p)]$ evaluates to $3/2$, while the right-hand side $D_R(\bar y\|p)+\overline{R(y)}-R(\bar y)$ evaluates to $5/8$. A second theorem in the same file proves, by `ring` and for arbitrary $R$, that the identity *does* hold under the standard convention $D_R(y\|p)=R(y)-R(p)-\langle\nabla R(p),y-p\rangle$ — so the mathematics is sound and the manuscript's §2.3 definition is what breaks it. The lemma also fails its own 'in particular' clause: under the §2.3 definition $p\mapsto\mathbb{E}_y[D_R(y\|p)]$ is not a proper scoring rule and is not minimised at $\bar y$, which is the property Lemmas 2.2, 3.2 and C.2 all consume.

For any $\mathbf{y} \in \Delta(\mathcal{P})$ and convex function $R : \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}$, let $\bar{y} = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[y]$, and $\overline{R(y)} = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[R(y)]$. For all $p \in \mathcal{P}$, $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathbf{y}}[D_R(y \| p)] = D_R(\bar{y} \| p) + \overline{R(y)} - R(\bar{y})$.

summary:
Verified the mathematics of *High-Dimensional Calibration from Swap Regret* end to end: 22 self-contained objects were extracted (definitions, lemmas, theorems, algorithm update rules, proof steps, and the abstract's quantitative claims), 16 reviewed informally and 6 routed to Lean 4. All six Lean snippets were settled — **4 REFUTED, 2 PASSED, 0 FAILED** — so no informal fallback pass was needed.

**What Lean settled.** Four machine-checked refutations, all with explicit witnesses. (1) Lemma 2.1's identity is false when read against the Bregman divergence as *defined* in §2.3 ($R(x)=x^4$, $\mathbf{y}$ uniform on $\{0,1\}$, $p=0$: $3/2 \neq 5/8$) — and a companion theorem proves it holds by `ring` for every $R$ under the standard convention, localising the defect to the definition line. (2) §2.4's definition of $\alpha$-strong convexity has its inequality reversed: $R(x)=x^2/2$, $\alpha=1$ satisfies the displayed condition yet violates the 'equivalent' bound $D_R(y\|p)\ge\alpha\|y-p\|^2$; Lean also verified that flipping the sign restores the equivalence. (3) Claim C.3 is stated with a $\ge$ where its proof derives and its use requires a $\le$, and its constant is $2T\,\mathrm{diam}^2/H^2$ where the proof reaches only $2T\,\mathrm{diam}^2/H$. (4) The closing parameter choice of Theorem 3.1, $L=12\rho/\epsilon$ and $H=\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{P})/\sqrt{\epsilon}$, yields $\tfrac52\epsilon T$, not $\epsilon T$ — Lean confirmed the repair $H = 2\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{P})/\sqrt{\epsilon}$ works. Two Lean proofs came back clean: Lemma C.4 ($\sum_{h=1}^H\|p_h-\tilde p_h\|^2 \le 2\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{P})^2$, proved in an arbitrary real normed space via $\tilde p_h - p_h = (y_h-p_h)/h$ and $\sum_h 1/h^2 \le 2-1/H$), and the full exponent chain of Theorem D.2.

**What informal review added.** Three further issues that no Lean statement could capture. Theorem 4.3 claims the lower bound up to $T\le\exp(c\,d^{1/7})$ while its own proof, Theorem 1.4, Theorem 4.1 and the $\ell_2$ analogue Theorem D.2 all give $d^{1/14}$. The abstract reports the simplex rate as $d^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ "significantly improving upon [Pen25]", whereas substituting $\rho=\log d$ into the abstract's own formula $\exp(O(\rho/\epsilon^2))$ gives $d^{O(1/\epsilon^2)}$ — which is exactly what §1.1 and Appendix E state, describing it as *recovering* [Pen25]; the abstract also overstates the lower bound as $\exp(\Omega(1/\epsilon))$ and claims a tightness that the two exponents cannot support. And §2.1's definition of $\mathrm{Cal}_T^D$ carries a $1/T$ that no other occurrence in the paper has and that would make Theorem 3.1 vacuous.

**No disagreements between verifiers.** Every Lean verdict was corroborated rather than contradicted by the informal reading, and no Lean run returned FAILED, so no verdict rests on a stalled proof search.

**Verdict.** CRITICAL_ERRORS. The architecture of the paper is sound — Lemma 2.2's reduction, the TreeCal/TreeSwap equivalence, Lemma 2.4, Lemma C.4, Lemma D.1 and the whole of Theorem D.2 all check out, and the constant-level defects in Claim C.3 and the proof of Theorem 3.1 are absorbed by the $O(\cdot)$ in the theorem statements. What earns the critical rating is that three *stated* objects assert something other than what the paper proves: the §2.3 Bregman definition and the §2.4 strong-convexity definition are both transposed or sign-flipped relative to every proof that consumes them (so Step 1 of the main proof does not follow from the hypotheses as written), Theorem 4.3 claims a strictly stronger exponent than its proof delivers, and the abstract advertises a rate and a tightness the body contradicts. A caveat on provenance: this manuscript is a markdown conversion, and several of the smaller items (the $1/T$, the missing $\sum$ in Lemma C.4's proof, the diameter subscript in Lemma 4.2) have the shape of transcription artefacts as much as authored errors; they are reported as what the document says.

Per `verify-math-lean`'s rule that a reused project is not the caller's to delete, it was kept (`lean_project_kept: true`); only the per-snippet scratch (`TMP.lean`, `claim.md`) was removed.
